title: From distress to eustress: why some stress is good for you
author: David Didau
summary: The relationship between stress and performance follows an inverted U-curve: too little stress produces apathy and shallow engagement, while too much overwhelms working memory and attention. Learning happens optimally in the uncomfortable middle ground where eustress—productive strain accompanying deliberate practice—creates cognitive demand without overwhelm. Students experience eustress through retrieval practice, explaining ideas rather than copying them, and public commitment (writing answers on whiteboards knowing they'll be seen). This cognitive demand strengthens memory and understanding. Teachers must intentionally design lessons to create this optimal stress level through checking attention and understanding, cold calling with no opt-out, and routines that force deliberate effort. The challenge is moving beyond eliminating stress as an educational toxin to recognizing productive stress as essential to effective learning.
points: Eustress (productive strain) accompanies deliberate practice and strengthens memory more than passive engagement
Learning happens at the inverted-U optimum: too little pressure creates apathy, too much overwhelms attention
Cold calling, retrieval practice, and public commitment create the cognitive demand needed for eustress
Students may experience lessons with high accountability and checking as 'stressful' but recognize the learning benefit
Teacher routines (mini whiteboards, checking for understanding, pausing for thinking) intentionally structure productive stress
quotes: Eustress is the productive strain that accompanies deliberate practice. The feeling students get when they are required to retrieve information rather than recognise it, to explain ideas rather than copy them.
The relationship between arousal and performance follows an inverted U-shaped curve. Too little pressure produces apathy and superficial engagement. Too much overwhelms attention and working memory.
Learning happens most reliably in the uncomfortable middle, where effort is required but success still feels attainable.
That cognitive demand is precisely what strengthens memory and understanding.

We are prone to treating stress as an educational toxin, something to be eliminated wherever possible. Yet the evidence suggests something more nuanced.” Archived from David Didau Substack on April 20, 2026 by Tim.
